LG-Q-221.rationale: Shorten the conspicuously long key and use nearby bank-capital misconceptions.
LG-Q-221.economicsRationale: Leverage means a small proportional asset loss can consume a large share of thin equity.
options: Small asset losses can exhaust bank capital.
Higher leverage requires a larger capital cushion.
Asset losses reduce deposits before bank capital.
Borrowing protects bank capital from asset losses.

LG-Q-226.rationale: Ask a direct policy-incentive question with parallel, economically related alternatives.
LG-Q-226.economicsRationale: IOR raises the return available on reserves and puts upward pressure on market rates; adding reserves need not guarantee easing.
LG-Q-226.q: The Fed adds reserves to support easier credit but raises the interest rate paid on reserve balances. Why might the higher reserve rate work against its objective?
options: It raises the return banks require from alternative lending.
It automatically removes the newly added reserve balances.
It lowers the return banks require from alternative lending.
It reduces the reserve requirement on bank deposits.
LG-Q-226.feedback: A higher return on reserve balances raises the opportunity cost of alternative lending and puts upward pressure on short-term rates. Adding reserves therefore does not by itself establish that credit conditions will ease.

LG-Q-306.rationale: Separate the effects of the two policy instruments without saying reserves are lent to the public.
LG-Q-306.economicsRationale: Bond purchases add reserve balances. Higher IOR puts upward pressure on short-term rates, so reserve quantity alone does not identify the stance.
LG-Q-306.q: The Fed buys bonds while raising the interest rate paid on reserve balances. Which conclusion follows?
options: Reserves rise, but the reserve-rate increase pushes short-term rates upward.
Reserves fall, and both actions push short-term rates downward.
Reserves rise, so short-term rates must fall despite the reserve-rate increase.
Reserves stay fixed because the higher reserve rate cancels the purchases.
LG-Q-306.feedback: Bond purchases add reserve balances. Raising the rate paid on those balances puts upward pressure on short-term market rates. The reserve increase alone does not establish the net effect on lending or spending.

LG-Q-311.rationale: State the hypothetical framework and distinguish capacity from incentives.
LG-Q-311.economicsRationale: Reserve requirements constrain expansion in this stipulated model; IOR changes the relative return to lending, not the legal reserve requirement.
LG-Q-311.q: In a hypothetical scarce-reserves system with a binding reserve requirement, which package combines actions that reduce lending capacity with incentives to reduce lending?
LG-Q-311.feedback: Bond sales reduce reserves and a higher reserve requirement reduces lending capacity in this model. A higher return on reserve balances also makes alternative lending less attractive.

LG-Q-312.rationale: State the hypothetical framework and distinguish capacity from incentives.
LG-Q-312.economicsRationale: Reserve requirements constrain expansion in this stipulated model; IOR changes the relative return to lending, not the legal reserve requirement.
LG-Q-312.q: In a hypothetical scarce-reserves system with a binding reserve requirement, which package combines actions that expand lending capacity with incentives to expand lending?
LG-Q-312.feedback: Bond purchases add reserves and a lower reserve requirement increases lending capacity in this model. A lower return on reserve balances also makes alternative lending more attractive.

ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9052.rationale: A familiar pair of shifts or short-run/long-run misconception requires linked reasoning, without Legendary multi-constraint synthesis.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9052.economicsRationale: The existing key remains correct; retain source-role metadata and move only the ordinary cognitive pool.
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9052.q: In a scarce-reserves textbook model, a student says, 'If the Fed buys bonds, inflation must rise immediately and real output cannot move.' Which correction is strongest?
ECON-SP-LEGENDARY-9052.feedback: In this textbook model, bond purchases lower interest rates and can raise aggregate demand and output while prices are sticky. Long-run monetary neutrality does not rule out that short-run response.

43285.q: In a closed-economy loanable-funds model, expected investment profitability falls while a larger budget deficit reduces planned national saving at every real interest rate. What must happen, and what remains uncertain?

43188.rationale: Distinguish an ordinary application from its one-step repair counterpart.
43188.economicsRationale: Public saving is 240−290=−50. With private saving 180, national saving is 130.
43188.q: Net tax revenue is $240, government purchases are $290, and private saving is $180. What is national saving, and how does the government budget affect it?
options: $130; the budget deficit reduces national saving.
$230; the budget deficit raises national saving.
$180; public saving does not enter national saving.
−$50; national saving equals public saving alone.
43188.feedback: Public saving is T − G = $240 − $290 = −$50. National saving adds private and public saving: $180 − $50 = $130. The deficit reduces the total.
43188.commonError: Treating public saving as the whole of national saving or reversing the deficit sign.

43202.rationale: A repair item asks one subtraction with the net-tax convention already supplied.
43202.economicsRationale: 500−450=50; Easy matches the actual task while the repair route stays intact.

ECON-NL-MEDIUM-162.rationale: Extend the repeated LFPR arithmetic to interpretation at its existing Medium tier.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-162.economicsRationale: 150/200=75%; the complement is outside the labor force, not necessarily unemployed.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-162.q: The labor force is 150 million and the adult population is 200 million. What is the labor-force participation rate, and what does the remaining share represent?
options: 75%; the remaining 25% are all unemployed.
50%; the remaining 50% are outside the labor force.
75%; the remaining 25% are outside the labor force.
66.7%; the remaining 33.3% are all unemployed.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-162.feedback: LFPR = 150/200 × 100 = 75%. The remaining 50 million adults are outside the labor force. Unemployed people who are actively seeking work belong to the labor force.
ECON-NL-MEDIUM-162.commonError: Confusing adults outside the labor force with unemployed active job seekers.

P52A-AS-B1-001.rationale: Restore a direct SRAS-shifter recognition task for the first checkpoint instead of duplicating a later two-horizon question.
P52A-AS-B1-001.economicsRationale: Higher contracted nominal wages raise production costs at each output price and shift SRAS left.
P52A-AS-B1-001.q: Firms sign new contracts that raise nominal wages. Productivity and other input prices are unchanged. What happens to short-run aggregate supply?
options: It shifts right.
It shifts left.
There is only a movement up the unchanged curve.
There is only a movement down the unchanged curve.
P52A-AS-B1-001.feedback: Higher nominal wages raise firms’ production costs at each price level, shifting short-run aggregate supply left.
P52A-AS-B1-001.commonError: Treating a change in nominal input costs as movement along an unchanged SRAS curve.

P52A-AS-B3-002.rationale: Remove an unused worker count; preserve the later checkpoint’s two-horizon task.
P52A-AS-B3-002.q: Nominal wage contracts are fixed. Actual output prices rise unexpectedly while other input prices are unchanged. Which initial response and later qualification are consistent with the sticky-wage account?

P52B-S4-STAB-B2-002.rationale: Replace a duplicate classification task with calculation and interpretation of a delayed fiscal expansion partly offset by automatic stabilizers; preserve the policy-mix/overheating repair skill.
P52B-S4-STAB-B2-002.economicsRationale: The total demand effects are already multiplied: +60−20=+40. With output initially at potential, automatic stabilizers only partly offset the delayed expansion. No second multiplication applies.
P52B-S4-STAB-B2-002.q: An economy has returned to potential output. At the current price level, a delayed purchases program would raise aggregate demand by $60 billion after all multiplier effects. Automatic stabilizers would reduce it by $20 billion, with no other changes. Does their response fully offset the program?
options: AD rises $40 billion; the program is only partly offset.
AD rises $80 billion; both changes add to demand.
AD is unchanged; automatic stabilizers fully offset the program.
AD falls $40 billion; automatic stabilizers more than offset the program.
P52B-S4-STAB-B2-002.feedback: The stated total effects give a net AD increase of $60 billion − $20 billion = $40 billion. Automatic stabilizers offset only part of the delayed program, so it can still add demand pressure after output has returned to potential.
P52B-S4-STAB-B2-002.commonError: Assuming automatic stabilizers fully cancel a delayed discretionary program, or adding effects that have opposite signs.

P52A-CPI-B3-003.rationale: Make the later CPI checkpoint test rebasing and interpretation instead of another basket-price substitution.
P52A-CPI-B3-003.economicsRationale: 132/120−1=10%; rebasing multiplies both indexes by 100/120, giving 100 and 110 without changing inflation.
P52A-CPI-B3-003.q: The CPI rises from 120 to 132. The statistical agency then makes the first of these years the base year, using the same fixed basket. What are the rebased indexes and the inflation rate, and does rebasing change measured inflation?
options: 100 and 112; inflation rises to 12%.
100 and 110; inflation remains 10%.
100 and 132; inflation rises to 32%.
120 and 132; inflation remains 12%.
P52A-CPI-B3-003.feedback: Multiply both indexes by 100/120. They become 100 and 110. Inflation is 132/120 − 1 = 110/100 − 1 = 10%; choosing a new index base does not change the price change.
P52A-CPI-B3-003.commonError: Confusing index-point changes with percentage inflation or treating rebasing as a price change.

PM2B2-BIAS-MB-002.rationale: Align the new-goods-bias checkpoint and its repair skill, replacing an unrelated substitution-bias duplicate.
PM2B2-BIAS-MB-002.economicsRationale: A price index that omits a newly available good may miss the benefit of expanded choice; no claim that every price falls.
PM2B2-BIAS-MB-002.q: A new product gives households an inexpensive alternative that did not previously exist, but the CPI basket will not include it for several years. Which cost-of-living benefit may the index initially miss?
options: The rise in prices of older products already in the basket.
The change in quantities when the fixed basket is priced again.
The benefit of satisfying wants through an expanded set of choices.
The automatic doubling of purchasing power from any new product.
PM2B2-BIAS-MB-002.feedback: A newly available good can let households achieve a given level of satisfaction at lower cost. Delayed inclusion can miss that benefit of expanded choice, a source of new-goods bias.
PM2B2-BIAS-MB-002.commonError: Ignoring the cost-of-living benefit of newly available choices.

PM2B2-BIAS-MB-003.rationale: Turn a repeated quality-change interpretation into a short calculation and interpretation.
PM2B2-BIAS-MB-003.economicsRationale: Price per service unit changes by 1.20/2=0.60, a 40% decrease.
PM2B2-BIAS-MB-003.q: A replacement appliance costs 20% more but provides twice the measured service, with no other relevant quality change. How does its price per unit of service compare with the old appliance?
options: It is 20% higher.
It is 40% lower.
It is 60% lower.
It is 80% higher.
PM2B2-BIAS-MB-003.feedback: For the same service, the relative price is 1.20/2 = 0.60. Price per unit of service falls 40%, even though the sticker price rises 20%.
PM2B2-BIAS-MB-003.commonError: Treating a sticker-price increase as inflation without adjusting for service quality.

PM2B3-SRC-EB-003.rationale: Use a direct technology task for the first checkpoint and its technological-knowledge repair skill.
PM2B3-SRC-EB-003.economicsRationale: More output from unchanged labor and equipment reflects improved methods, rather than capital deepening.
PM2B3-SRC-EB-003.q: A factory discovers a production method that yields more output with the same workers and equipment. Which source of productivity growth does this illustrate?
options: More physical capital per worker.
An increase in natural resources.
A larger labor force.
Improved technological knowledge.
PM2B3-SRC-EB-003.feedback: A better method raises output from existing inputs. This is improved technological knowledge rather than an increase in the amount of labor or equipment.
PM2B3-SRC-EB-003.commonError: Confusing improved production methods with more physical inputs.

P52B-S4-UNEM-B2-003.rationale: Test employment-to-unemployment flows at the existing Medium checkpoint instead of duplicating a discouraged-worker classification item.
P52B-S4-UNEM-B2-003.economicsRationale: Employment falls from 300 to 270 and unemployment rises from 30 to 60; labor force stays 330 and UR=18.18%.
P52B-S4-UNEM-B2-003.q: An economy has 300 employed and 30 unemployed people. Thirty employed people lose their jobs and immediately begin actively seeking work. No one enters or leaves the labor force. What happens to the unemployment rate?
options: It rises from about 9.1% to about 18.2%.
It stays at about 9.1% because the labor force is unchanged.
It rises from 10% to 20% because employment is the denominator.
It falls from about 9.1% to about 8.3% because the labor force grows.
P52B-S4-UNEM-B2-003.feedback: Initially, UR = 30/(300+30) ≈ 9.1%. Job losses move 30 people from employment to unemployment without changing the labor force: UR = 60/330 ≈ 18.2%.
P52B-S4-UNEM-B2-003.commonError: Using employment as the unemployment-rate denominator or assuming job loss increases the labor force.
